passages.t: The prophet whose sign comes true
passages.happening:
Moses sets out three cases. Each is about someone who urges Israel to worship other gods.

The first is a prophet. “If a prophet or dreamer of dreams arises among you and proclaims a sign or wonder to you, and if the sign or wonder he has spoken to you comes about, but he says, ‘Let us follow other gods (which you have not known) and let us worship them,’ you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer” (verses 1-3).

Moses gives the reason. “For the LORD your God is testing you to find out whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul” (verse 3). Israel is to follow the LORD, fear him, keep his commands, ‘serve Him and hold fast to Him’ (verse 4).

Then the penalty. “Such a prophet or dreamer must be put to death, because he has advocated rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery” (verse 5). “So you must purge the evil from among you.”
passages.hearers:
Prophets and dreamers were familiar figures all over the ancient world. Letters from the city of Mari on the Euphrates, from the eighteenth century BC, report messages from prophets and dreams sent to the king. Israel was not unusual in having prophets. What this chapter adds is a test.

One test of a prophet is whether his words come true. Chapter 18 will give that test. This case is harder. Here the sign does come about. The prophet has, as people say, results. And still he is not to be followed.

The test is what he says about God. If his message is ‘other gods’, no wonder can make it true. A miracle does not prove a message. Israel already knows who its God is: the one ‘who brought you out of the land of Egypt’. Anything that leads away from him is false, however impressive it looks.

Verse 3 gives a second way of seeing it. God is testing Israel. The words are those of the Shema: does Israel love him ‘with all your heart and with all your soul’? Love is shown when something attractive pulls the other way.

The Hebrew word translated ‘rebellion’ in verse 5 means revolt against a rightful ruler. That is the key to the law. In Israel the LORD was king, and the covenant with him was the nation's foundation. To call the people to other gods was to call for the overthrow of the king. The law treats it as a nation treats treason.

This chapter has a close parallel outside the Bible. In 672 BC the Assyrian king Esarhaddon bound his subjects by oath to report any word of revolt against his heir, whether it came from a relative or a brother, from a prophet or one who consults oracles. Many scholars think this chapter takes up the language of such oaths and turns it: that kind of loyalty belongs to the LORD and not to the king of Assyria. Scholars who date the book earlier point to the older tradition of treaties going back to the Hittites.

The refrain ‘purge the evil from among you’ recurs through these laws. The Hebrew verb means to burn away.
passages.later:
Chapter 18 gives the other test of a prophet: “When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken” (Deuteronomy 18:22).

Jesus warned his followers in the terms of this passage: “For false Christs and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders that would deceive even the elect, if that were possible” (Matthew 24:24).

John tells the church to do the testing: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1).

Paul takes the refrain of verse 5 and uses it for something very different from death. A man living in open sin is to be put out of the church's fellowship: ‘Expel the wicked man from among you’ (1 Corinthians 5:13). In the same breath he says, “God will judge those outside.”

The Gospels record that this law was turned against Jesus. Some in the crowd said of him, ‘No, He deceives the people’ (John 7:12).
passages.hard:
How can the Bible command death for urging people to worship another god?

The law says what it says, and a reader who values freedom of belief is right to find it hard. It should be read soberly and inside its setting.

Interpreters make several points. Many note that Israel was a nation unlike any other, in covenant with God as its king. To promote other gods there was treason against the foundation of the nation's life, and nations ancient and modern have treated attempts at their overthrow in that way. Others stress that these laws required careful inquiry and more than one witness (verse 14; 17:6), and that the Old Testament rarely records them being carried out. Others see them as belonging to one stage in God's dealings with his people, which is not carried over into the New Testament.

On what follows for today, Christians broadly agree. These penalties are not given to the church. The New Testament puts no sword in its hand. It meets false teaching with teaching, with discipline inside its own fellowship, and with prayer, and it leaves judgment to God. Paul says that a servant of the Lord ‘must gently reprove those who oppose him’ (2 Timothy 2:25). Jesus told of a farmer who would not let his servants pull up weeds, in case they pulled up wheat: “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Matthew 13:30).

So it must be said plainly. No church and no state may use this chapter against anyone. It gives no one the right to kill, punish, threaten or silence a person for what he believes or teaches.

That needs saying because it has been done. There were periods when Christians used chapters like this one to justify persecution. Most Christians today regard that as a grave misreading. It was a wrong done in God's name.

What the chapter still teaches is how serious it is to lead another person away from God. It does not teach force.
passages.asks: The prophet in this passage gets results, and his message is still false. Ask how you judge a teacher or a movement: by what it can show, or by whether it leads you toward the God who has made himself known. And ask what attractive thing is testing, at present, whether you love God with your whole heart.

passages.t: When the voice is someone you love
passages.happening:
The second case comes closer. “If your very own brother, or your son or daughter, or the wife you embrace, or your closest friend secretly entices you, saying, ‘Let us go and worship other gods’” (verse 6), whether the gods of nearby peoples or distant ones, “you must not yield to him or listen to him” (verse 8).

The law then requires that such a person be put to death by stoning, with the one who was enticed casting the first stone (verses 9-10). The reason is given again: he tried ‘to turn you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery’ (verse 10).

“Then all Israel will hear and be afraid, and will never again do such a wicked thing among you” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The list in verse 6 names the nearest ties a person had: a full brother, a child, a wife, and the friend who is, in the Hebrew, like one's own soul. The word ‘secretly’ matters. The prophet of the first case spoke in public. This is a whisper at home, from someone trusted.

The point of naming these people is that no bond may rank above loyalty to God. In an ancient society religion was bound up with family, clan and town. To worship other gods was not a private choice. It touched the whole community's standing before the God who had made a covenant with them.

This is one of the hardest laws in the book to read. It asks a person to act against someone he loves. The text does not pretend otherwise. ‘Show him no pity’ is said because pity is exactly what a person would feel.

The rule that the accuser's hand must be first had a purpose. It laid the weight on the one who brought the charge. A person could not accuse in secret and leave the killing to others. Together with the rule of two or three witnesses in chapter 17, it worked against false charges.

These were laws for ancient Israel under its covenant. The hard question on verses 1 to 5 sets out how Christians read them, and says what must be said about today.
passages.later:
Jesus kept the claim of this passage and removed the stones. He said, “Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me” (Matthew 10:37). He asks for first place above every family tie. He gave his followers no penalty to carry out.

When two of his disciples wanted to call down fire on a village that refused him, “Jesus turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55).

Peter writes of how a believer is to live with a husband who does not share her faith. It is not by force or by leaving him to judgment. It is so that he ‘will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives’ (1 Peter 3:1).
passages.hard:
Does this passage give anyone the right to harm, shun or threaten a family member who leaves the faith or follows another?

No. This was a law of ancient Israel, given to a nation in covenant with God as its king. It is not given to the church, to any family, or to any state. No one may use it to justify violence, threats or cruelty toward a relative or friend because of what that person believes.

Killing, beating or imprisoning a family member over religion is a grave evil, and nothing in the Christian faith permits it. The New Testament's instruction for a home divided over faith is patience, prayer and a good life.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The hardest pull away from God may come from the people a person loves most, and it usually comes quietly. Ask whose approval you would find it hardest to lose for the sake of your faith. And ask how you treat those close to you who do not believe as you do. Jesus asks for first place in your heart. He does not ask you to stop loving them.

passages.happening:
The third case is a whole town. Israel hears that ‘wicked men’ have led the people of one of its own cities to serve other gods (verses 12-13).

The first duty is to find out: ‘you must inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly’ (verse 14). Only if the charge is established with certainty does the law go on.

Then the town is to be put to the sword and devoted to destruction, with its livestock. All its goods are to be piled in the square and burned with the town, ‘as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God’ (verse 16). It is to stay a ruin and never be rebuilt.

“Nothing devoted to destruction shall cling to your hands” (verse 17). Then God will turn from his anger, show mercy and compassion, and multiply the people as he swore.
passages.hearers:
The three cases have widened: one public figure, one member of the family, one whole community.

The town in this law is an Israelite town. That is important for how the hard chapters of this book are read. The ban, the giving over to complete destruction, is the same word used for the nations of Canaan in chapter 7. Here it falls on Israel's own. It was never a matter of one race against another. The measure was the worship of other gods, and Israel was held to it as strictly as anyone.

Three verbs stand at the door of this law: inquire, investigate, interrogate. A rumor is not enough. The matter must be ‘established with certainty’. The law that names so severe a penalty fences it with a demand for proof.

Nothing from the town could be kept. Everything was burned. So no one could grow rich by accusing a neighbor town. The law removes the motive of gain.

The men who lead the town astray are called, in Hebrew, sons of beliyya'al, which means worthless men. In later Jewish writing the word became a name for an evil power, and Paul uses it so (2 Corinthians 6:15).

The Old Testament rarely records these laws being carried out. In Judges 19 to 21 the tribes use this chapter's language against the town of Gibeah, for a different crime, and the war that follows nearly destroys the tribe of Benjamin.

The hard question on verses 1 to 5 sets out how Christians read these penalties. They are no warrant for any church or state to act against any person or community.
passages.later:
The book of Judges uses the language of this chapter when the tribes demand the men of Gibeah: ‘so we can put them to death and purge Israel of this evil’ (Judges 20:13).

Paul says that the church fights in another way altogether: “The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world” (2 Corinthians 10:4). And Jesus said to the governor who tried him, “My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight” (John 18:36).
passages.asks: Before anything else, the law required careful inquiry: three verbs for finding out the truth. Ask how quickly you believe a bad report about a person or a group, and how much you check before you repeat it. And notice that Israel was judged by the standard it applied to others. Ask whether you hold yourself to the measure you use for people outside your own circle.
